From H timer and Smith's European Times, October 17, 1819. The English public have heard with extreme regret of the sudden and unlooked for dispute w hich lias arisen between the French and American Governments, and the consequent rupture of their diplomatic relations. The various unauthenticated statements brought by the packet of the origin of tliis very untimely quarrel are too vague and contradictory to enable us to form a correct opinion of its real character and merits. But quite sufficient litis transpired to show that it is either a simple question of pounds, shillings, and pence, or that it springs out of some trifling cause connected with the conduct and deport-

ment of one or other of the diplomatic representatives of either or both of the Republics. To assume that the rr.opLt of France intend to insult the confederation of the United States, or that the people of America seek to offer an affront to the French nation by any particular ambassadorial appointment, would be the height of absurdity. Each Republic is too powerful, too conscious of what is due to itself to commit w ilfully any such wanton breach of those laws of courtesy and honour which keep the highest civilised nations upon terms of mutual self-respect and unity. We therefore at once dismiss from our minds any apprehensions of the result. Instead of seeking to widen the breach, or of further estranging the two parties, w e are sure we speak the sentiments of the people of England, and certainly our own, when we express our readiness to do everything in our power to heal the wounded pride of the offended party, and to promote a sincere and speedy reconciliation. It is scarcely fifteen years ago when it w as Lord Pahiicrston's peculiar good fortune to mediate successfully between France and the United States, when war between the two countries was imminent, from the refusal of the French Chambers to pay the American indemnities. Compared with Ungrate circumstances of that time, the present misunderstanding appears to have arisen from the most trivial causes. The same desire to promote peace, which at that time urged Lord Palmerston to bring about happily a re-estab-

lislnnent of friendly relations between the excited disputants, w ill, we are sure, animate his lordship again, on the present occasion, to exert his influence to bring about a reconciliation. The alleged grounds of the dispute furnish no sufficient pretext for either party to have recourse to arms ; and, at this moment, when we hoped that the Hags of the United States, and of France and England, would be unfurled, if required, in the .Mediterranean to protect the Sultan of Turkey against the oppression and insidious aggression of the Emperor of Russia, it would, indeed, be a deplorable misfortune for the whole world if two Republics, who are looked up to as the champions of freedom, should lix upon this inopportune moment to break out into a most untimely quarrel. Tlte news taken out to the United States hv the last packet will, we are sure, operate effectually upon all the influential men in America to do everything in their power to compose this difference, without making any concession inconsistent with their national honour and independence. The people of France are little disposed to rush into a war, when the battle-field must be on the other side of the Atlantic. Never, at any previous period, was il more essential that a complete accord should exist amongst all the great liberal Governments of the world.

From Wilmer and Smith's European Times, October 17, 1819. The threatened rupture between) Russia and Austria and Turkey has been the chief topic amongst all classes of the community, and in its paramount importance the Roman difficulty is almost lost sight of The stand taken by the French ambassador at Constantinople was not so decided or dignified as Sir Stratford Canning's ; but there is little doubt that, whatever steps Great Britain takes, she will be fully seconded, if not by Louis Napoleon, at least by the French people. A correspondent residing at Paris thus writes on the subject : þÿ " The Turkish question is still touched on cautiously. The Legitimists do not wish to see France at war with Russia. The Thiers party would only desire it on condition of heirs; allowed to conduct the war themselves The republicans, anxious for the glory of the Republic, are ready to enter the field. The Steele is quite sure that the Lmperor of Russia cannot draw back, and the National holds that war is inevitable. The latter paper distrusts Louis Napoleon, believing that he is secretly seeking the sup port of the Czar The President can now prove his sincerity, by sustaining his Cabinet, which will not blench, if allowed the exercise of its dispositions, 'l'liete can be no doubt, should the present Ministry be able to main tain itself, that Lord Normanby's diplomatic task will be easy. Should the Legitimists come into power, difficulties would most likely spring up, such as may not at present be considered probable. The Legitimists are filled with animosity against M. Dufaure

and his friends, a!! of whom do not appear to be animated bv bis courageous spirit M. Passy and M. do Tracy take gloomy views of the situation, and express a strong desire to resign. The state of the finances weighs as heavily on the public mind as on that of the Finance Minister, and prevents so ardent an expression of feeling on the Turkish question as might have teen expected. The satisfaction fell, however, at the conduct of the Rrilish and French ambassadors at Constantinople is very great amongst nil but the

It is whispered annul that they have made a conquest of M. de Lainartine, and have his name on their ministerial list. The feeling displayed hv the London papers in reference to the conduct of the British and French ambassadors at Constantinople, greatly pleased the Bourse, and tended to relieve the gloom which bad been hanging over the market. The only pro- Russian party in France is the parti pretre Bourbonists. It is said to be the intention of the French Government to interfere in the nllair of the extradition of the Hungarian refugees in Turkey. Nothing hut that affair is said to be the reason of the mission of M. Gustave de Beaumont to Vienna." General Lamoriciere's mission to Russia having proved a failure, he has left St. Petersburg on Iris return to Paiis. He was received by the Emperor with perfect good breeding, but this cordiality was only intended to him in his military character. As ambassador of the French Republic, the Lmperor would hold no communication with General de Latnorioii'ro. Ho was provided with a double set ol þÿcredentials the one as atnbas- >ador, tlie other as minister-plenipotentiary: and the great object of the mission was the hope that the Lnq oror would receive him as

U\ <0 3i 0 I Z A T I 3« ambassador. But the Emperor never gave him an opportunity of producing the latter credentials, or alluding in any way to the subject. General de Lumoi iciere, therefore, returns to France without having an opportunity of speaking one word to the Emperor on political matteis. and lite only memorial he will bring back ol his mission is the recollection ol sundry reviews, and the splendid suit of Circassian armour presented to him by Nicholas immediately alter iiis arrival at the imperial head quarters. Considering that the President of the Republic went so far, in his endeavours to procure a favourable reception for General de Lamoricieie, as to banish the unfortunate Polish refugees tesident in France, tins result is a poor one, but it is to be hoped it will he a lesson to the President of the Republic (whose experience in diplomacy is as yet not very extensive) that it is not by such concessions as the expulsion ol a few inoffensive refugees that lie can hope to gain the lespeci of Europe, or even the support of Russia. The President has, in fact, profited by the lesson, for he has already expressed his indignation at the attempt made bv Russia to torce Turkey to give up the Hungarian refugees, and his determination to go fieart and hand with Eng land in resisting so preposterous a demand.

From the Nett York Herald, November 12, Important from llie Sanilirich IilatMA. S\n Francisco. September 3ft, ) Sunday Night, half past !). j I write to inform you that I have just received news from the Sandwich Islands. The French came in on the 25th August, and oil the 2Gth took possession of tha fort and towns of Oahu and Honolulu. Business was suspended for two days. The Sandwich Islanders did not resist. They seized on the newspaper olticcs and consequently there are no papers. 1 tried to get them, but there w ere none. Every thing quiet when the bark Mary Frances left there, the 5th of September. The Pacific News of the 2!)th of September, gives the follow ing additional information: þÿ þÿ In our paper of Saturday last we announced that a rumor was in circulation that a difficulty bad arisen at the Sandwich Islands, between (lie French Consul General and the Hawaiian government. Since that time the French frigate, the Poursuivante, under i lie command of Admiral Trominelin, lias arrived at this port from the Sandwich Islands, which place she left early in the present, month, bringing, as we learn, Mr. Dillon, the French Consul, and bis family, as passengers. It is said that Mr. Dillon lias finally closed bis mission at the Islands, and that be proceeds to France, through the United 8tatcs, taking passage in the steamer about leaving for Panama. þÿ The Poursuivante brings despatches, we believe, for Commodore Jones and tor the State Department at Washington. The contents of these are of course not yet made public; but we

learn from the reports in circulation about tow n, and which, so litr as we know, are not disputed, that the transactions which took place at the Island before the French frigate left, were in general as follows: þÿ The demands of the French Consul þÿ the most important of which related to the importation of French brandies into the Islands, at reduced rates of duty, and to the sale of

ardent spirits by French whalers, visiting the þÿ ments were refused by the Hawaiian ports of the Islands for refreshgovernment, on the ground that its existing regulations on these subjects were in conformity to tire text and spirit of tin treaty concluded between the French government and that, of the islands.'þÿ There were, however, several other matters in issue, and the Hawaiian government, we understand, was desirous to submit the whole case for decision, to the cabinet at l'aris. This mode of adjusting the matter, Mr. Dillon and the admiral did not see tit to accept. It is also understood that the Hawaiian authorities w. re willing to avail themselves of the offered mediation of the ilritish Consul Cenera! in the premises þÿ and that this also was declared by the French Consul and admiral, who insisted upon a ddinite compliance with 1 heir demands

brief specified time. þÿ Such compliance being refused on the part of the islands, the French Admiral, against the protest, as we understand, of the American Consul (the diplomatic intercourse between the Islands government and Mr. 'fen Fyek, the American Commissioner, not having been resumed, we believe, since its suspension some mouths ago,) proceeded to forcible measures. The Hawaiian fort was seized, disarmed, its ammunition destroyed, and the Hawaiian (lag lowered for about three days, when the French occupation of the fort ceased, and the Hawaiian (lag was again raised. One of the public vessels ofthc Hawaiian government was also seized by the French and sent off, under French control, to Tahita or Valparaiso. The French authorities then left the Islands. þÿ It appears to us difficult to understand upon what grounds the course of action, oil the pa rt of the French authorities, can be justified, and equal! difficult to see what good or useful result, of anv kind, has been accomplished hv it. If the Hawaiian authorities were in the right in the controversy, under the treaty stipulations, then the course of the French was plainly an unjustifiable aggression upon the weak and defenceless. If, on the other hand, the Hawaiian government was in the wrong,
mediation unsuitable, could not the'ease have been submitted to the French cabinet, for decision, as the Hawaiian government is understood to have desired and þÿproposed.

II. 41. Kcutsch. Politeness. þÿ Care should be taken to cultivate, in all intercourse with friends, gentle and obliging manners. It is a common error to suppose that familiar intimacy supersedes attention to the lesser duties of behaviour; and that, under the notion of freedom, it may excuse a careless, or even a rough demeanour. þÿ Un the conlrary, an intimate connexion can only he perpetuated by a constant endeavour to he l'1 easing and agreeable. 'Flu same behaviour which procures friendship, is absolutely necessary to the preservation of it. Let no harshness, no appearance of neglect, no supercilious affection of superiority be encouraged in the intercourse of friends. A tart reply, a proneness to rebuke, a captious ami contradictory spirit, are often known to embitter domestic life, and to set friends at variance; it is only by continuing courtesy and urbanity of behaviour, that we long preserve the comforts of friendship. You must often have observed, that nothing, is so strong a recommendation, on it slight acquaintance, as politeness; nor does it lose its value by time or intimacy, when preserved as it ought to be, in the nearest connexions and strictest friendships. In general, propriety of behaviour must be the fruit of instruction, of observation, arid reasoning ; and it is to be cultivated and improved like any other branch of knowledge or virtue. Particular inodes and ceremonies of behaviour 'try in different places. Those can only be learned by observation on the man-

ners of those who are best skilled in them. Rut the principles of politeness are the same in all places. Wherever there are human beings, it must be impolite to hurt the temper, or pain the feelings ol those with whom you converse. By raising people up, instead of mortifying and depressing them, we make ourselves so many friends in place of enemies. Mrs. Chaponf..

From the J\e.w York Herald, November 12. The G olden Emigration. We have no data by which to show conclusively the emigration to California overland this year, but our accounts from the north represent the entire body in a prosperous and healthful state. þÿ We are enabled to add that about one fifth are already in the country", and the remainder vigorously pressing forward, in companies which are every day pouring into the Sacramento valley. The arrivals for the month ending Sept. 28, at this port, by sea, are as follows : þÿ Americans 4,271 Foreigners 1,531

Total 5,802 Of which 122 are females. Number of tons of shipping in the harbor of San Francisco, this day, 94,344. From the Alta California, Sept. 13. It is necessary that we should state, in order to relieve anxieties and allay the tears which have been but unduly created, regarding the general prosperity of the emigration overland this year, t hat latest accounts are highly encouraging, and represent the entire body full five weeks earlier than the emigration of any preceding year. We deem this statement hut just in view of the wrong impression which has gone abroad, and which exists even to the present time to a great extent in this place. The friends of emigrating parties residing in the States may rest assured of the general safety of till, and that aside from the ordinary fatigue and privations of the journey, no suffering has as yet been experienced. About 30,000 persons, mostly young men, compose the overland emigration this year. A portion of this body is already in the country, and parties are nearly every day arriving. Captain R. Owen, who piloted a company across the country by the Sante þÿl route, e diverging to the northern road, crossing the Sierra Nevada, and entering California near þÿJohnson s rancho, reports the emigration in an unusually forward state, with provisions plenty and to spare. þÿ þÿ I liegrass along the road had been abundant, and but in one place was it believed a scarcity of food for stock would he encountered. This was above the sink of þÿMary river, s and here, by

abandoning the road a subsistence can be procured. We are not among those who suppress a motive of charity, nor throw an obstacle in the way of so holy a work as that of the rescue of our þÿ countrymen in þÿdistress, from any real impending danger. In this case we cannot conceive the propriety of circulating misrepresentations, and exciting undue sympathy. Let precautionary measures be adopted 1o relieve suffering, and we have acted our part. The emigrants are pressing on bravely and well. Gold is the gaol, and the beck of fortune is a power impellent. We do not apprehend distress, nor can wc but eschew the method of awakening public, sympathy, which sacrifices private feelings.

If a toucan he yelping in the neighbourhood, the cassique drops liis song and imitates him : then he will amuse his protector with the cries of the different species of the woodpecker ; and when the sheep bleat, he will distinctly answer them ; then comes liis own song again ; and if a puppy dog or a Guinea-fowl interrupt him, he takes it off admirably, and by his different gestures during the time, you would conclude that he enjoys the sport. The cassique is gregarious, and imitates any sound he hears with such exactness, that he goes by no other name than that of mocking-bird among the colonists. At breeding time, a number of these pretty c horisters resort to a tree near the þÿplanter house, s and from its outside brandies weave their pendulous nests. ,So conscious do they seem thnt they never give offence, and so little suspicious are they of receiving any injury from man, that they will choose a tree within forty yards irom liis house,

and occupv the branches so low down, that he may peep into their nests. A tree in Warratiila Greek affords a proof of this. The proportions of the cassique are so fine, that he may he said to he a model of symmetry in ornithology. On each wing lie lias a bright yellow spot ; his belly and half the tail are of the same colour; all the rest of the body is black ; his beak is the colour of sulphur hut it fades in death, and requires the same operation as the bill of the toucan to make it keep its colour. The ease, elegance, and rapidity of liis movements, the animation of liis eye, and the intelligence he displays in listening to and laying up lessons from almost every species of the feathered creation within his hearing, are really surprising, and mark the peculiarity of liis genius. This bird is easily domesticated and taught artificial tunes. \V A TEUTON.

Respect rou the aged. þÿ It happened at Athens, during a public representation of some play, exhibited in honour of the state, that an old gentleman came too late for a place suitable to his age and quality. A number of young men, who observed the difficulty and confusion the poor old gentleman was in, made signs to him, that they would accommodate him, if lie came where they snt. The good man bustled through the crowd accordingly ; hut when he came to the seats to which he was invited, the jest among the young fellows

was to sit close, and expose the confusion and embarrassment of the old man to the gaze of the whole audience. This frolic went round all the benches reserved for the Athenians. But, on those occasions, there were also particular places set apart for strangers. When the good man, covered with confusion, came towards the boxes appointed for the Lacedemonians, these honest, though less instructed people, rose from their seats, and with the greatest respect, received the old gentleman among them. þÿ The Athenians, being suddenly touched with a sense of the Lacedemonians virtue and their own misconduct, gave a thunder of applause ; and the old man cried out. þÿ The \thcnians understand what is good, but the Lacedemonians practise þÿit. The Mate Convention. Prom tlie Aid California, October 1 'I'his liodv, up to our latest dates, had been in session a little over three w eeks. Most of the provisions of the proposed constitution had been acted and passed upon in committee of the whole, and that, we suppose, may he taken as a fair index of what will he the action of the house. The Dili of rights, as adopted in committee of the whole, embraces twenty sections, of the usual character of such provisions. The only point upon which it was supposed a controversy would arise þÿ the question of slavery þÿ passed without debate, and unanimously, utterly prohibiting slavery. Some were in favor of submitting the matter to the people for a separate vote; hut it was not contended for with any show of strenuosity, and was voted dow n almost unanimously. 'flit suffrage question was t lie source of considerable debate ; hut was finally disposed of by admitting all male citizens of the United States, six months resident in California, and twenty-one years ol age, (Indians, Africans, and the descendants of Africans, excepted,) to the privileges of electors.

The Legislature is to consist ol two branches, an assembly and a senate, w ith such general powers, privileges, and duties, as are usually given to such bodies. Hanking corporations and lotteries are prohibited, and all other corporations, except for municipal purposes, are to he established under general laws, the stockholders to be individually liable for all debts. Some considerable debate occurred upon a provision which allows corporations to he formed for receiving deposits of gold and silver. it was urged that, under such a provision, an irresponsible system of hanking might grow up; hut tin section was finally so amended as to answer all objections, and, in that shape, passed. The members of the assembly are to he elected annually, and the members of tin senate arii to hold their offices for two years. One half of the senate is to he elected each year. No person can he a member of the legislature w ho has not been a resident of the State one year, in addition to other qualifications. The number of members of assembly is never to he less than twenty-four, nor more than thirtv-six, until the number of inhabitants in this State shall amount to one hundred thousand ; and after that period at such ratio that the w hole number of members of assembly shall never he less than thirty, nor more than eighty. The senate is never to consist of less than one-third, nor more than one-half the number of the assembly. Some division of opinion arose on a proposition made by Mr. MrUarver, to

prevent free persons of color from settling in California, and also to prevent slaveholders from bringing slaves into the Slate, for the purpose of liberating them. It finally passed in committee of the whole; hut it lias been looked upon since as jeopardizing the ratitlcation of the constitution by Congress; and as this feeling was gaining ground, the house, probably, w ill strike it out. A governor, lieutenant-governor, secretary of state, comptroller, treasurer, attorney-general, and surveyor-general, constitute the executive department. þÿ They an all to hold their offices for two years. The governor and lieutenantgovernor are to he elected by general ballot ; the secretary of state is to he appointed by the governor, by and with the advice and consent of the senate; the comptroller, and three other State officers are to he elected by the legislature in joint ballot for the first term, and afterwards by the people at the general State election. An effort was made in ihe committee of the whole to strike out the office of comptroller, but it failed. It will, however, he again pressed in the house, and as the office is totally unnecessary, we trust the motion w ill he successful. The governor has the usual powers, including the veto, and the privileges and duties of his office do not vary materially from those of all other States in the Union. The other State officers correspond in duties and powers with those generally ascribed them.

Tlu- article relative to the militia, as passed in committee ot' the 'tv hole, is substantially such as is lburid in other state const it irt ions, as is that also relative to amendments. The boundary, indicia!, and educational questions were not decided upon at Inst advices, but it was supposed the convention would adjourn in all the first week in October. þÿ New N ork Herald.

Whenever we behold a tear, let our kindliest sympathies awake þÿ let it have a sacred claim upon all that we can do to succour and comfort under affliction. \\ h;,t rivers of tears have down, excited by the cruel and perverse ways of man ! THE Danish School House being now evacuated by the military men and restored to the use of the instruction, it is hereby made known, that, as the necessary repairs will soon be finished, the School will be moved to this its oi iginal place on the first of December next. The branches of instruction are: Catechism and Bible History, Danish and English Reading and Grammar, History, Geography, Arithmetic and Writing. In addition to these instructions, if desired, will be privately given in the German oe French languages, as well as in Geometry and Geometrical Drawing, without any increase of pay, which is, for one scholar a month fixed to be one dollar, for two brothers or sisters one dollar and a half, for three and upwards two dollars. Parents and Guardians are therefore desired to send their Children to this establishment, to the prosperous state of which the teachers will devote their joint efforts. Alex: Itramll, Chief-teacher of the School. Frederiksted 1 4th cf November 1849.

Bui what has been witnessed t No less than thirteen Hungarian generals wi o it livered themselves up at tiie close of the war, and induced their .soldiers to lay down their arms, have been mar: reit under the guise of a court-martial ; and to make the tragedy display a suit able denouement, Count Battyany, Prime Minister of Hungary, has been shot under circumstances whic h will for ever make the Austrian name synonymous with cruelty, treachery, and di. mour. From the St. Thomas Times, Nov. 28, 1849. The Great Western arrived here on Saturday afternoon from Now York, her dates are from that city to the 12th and the European Mail received by her at Bermuda to the 2nd inst. We arc compelled to condense our summary as follows : þÿ The London Morning Herald publishes on the authority of a þÿ reliable þÿsource an announcement intimating the determination of His Majesty, King Freiierik vii and his Government, of agreeing to no proposition for the division of Schlesvig, being resolved on the indivisibility of the Duchy. Count Moltke had arrived at St. Petersburgh, where His Majesty had despatched him on an extraordinary mission. The former Austrian ambassador Baron von Langenau, had arrived at Copenhagen; lie is said to be the Bearer of the order of St. Stephen from the Austrian Court to our sovereign. The Times Berlin correspondent writes thus : þÿ þÿ The German fleet has been a constant source of dilemma, and its brief history is the oddest in naval annals. þÿ it was commenced by agreeing on its Hag, and appointing its Admiral who was forthwith decorated for the future victories he was to gain as soon as he

should be in possession of ships and crews. Tributes and steamers were then ordered without funds, the attempts to raise whic h were praiseworthy, but ins'illicient. Tiie ladies begged persevenngly, and worked immense quantities of cushions and footstools in Berlin wool for bazaars and lotteries, in vain ; and when some ships were procured on the credit of Prussia it was found there was no harbour to keep them in. It was proposed to make them over to Austria, and send them to lay up in the Mediterranean, thus placing the whole continent of Mu rope between them and their only possible enemy þÿ the Danes ; but this measure was very unpopular, and Belgium was resorted to, and the (Herman fleet is to þÿ sleep on its þÿshadow in the basins of Antwerp. As if to prove its humility, it had nothing to do with the one naval capture the Germans made during the war, for the action with the Gefion at Eckcrnlbrde was fought by infantry, dragoons, and two land batteries ; and at the present moment there prevails the greatest anxiety as to the latter vessel. It is suspected the Danes have evil designs upon her, as some ships of war have been seen hovering about the mouth of the creek, watching an opportunity for a corp de þÿmain.
